A fourth objection is that consumer antivirus and mobile-security apps – products such as Kaspersky, Avast, and Norton, alongside Google's built-in Play Protect – already let an owner detect compromise. These are real and widely used: Play Protect is, in Google's description, "the most widely deployed mobile threat protection service in the world" and "scans 200 billion Android apps daily" [4]. But all of them, however privileged, run inside the very system they are meant to vet. The third-party products operate as ordinary applications, while Play Protect is more privileged still – a component of Google Mobile Services that reaches across the device to disable or remove other apps on the owner's behalf [123], [34] – yet it too executes within the running operating system rather than from any external, trusted vantage. They match applications and files against known-malware signatures and heuristics within the storage the operating system permits them to see – Kaspersky's full scan, for instance, covers "the device's entire file system" [3] – which catches known, application-level threats but presupposes an operating system that is reporting truthfully about itself.

The vendors say as much. Avast states the limit plainly: "Like all applications on the Android market, it is subject to limitations imposed by the operating system version running on the device. It cannot protect against exploits targeting specific vulnerabilities in the OS kernel, the network stack and other fundamental parts of the system." [124] That is exactly the class of compromise owner-inspectability concerns: a kernel-level or sub-operating-system implant sits beneath the vantage point these tools occupy and can neutralize or evade an in-system scanner whatever its privileges, as Sections 9 and 14 develop. Consumer antivirus therefore catches the known and the application-level but does not supply the external, trusted vantage point verification requires – narrowing the gap for commodity malware without closing it for the targeted, low-level compromise, and so confirming rather than refuting the thesis.

13. Owner-Controlled Inspection and the Secure-Root Gap

The objections above return repeatedly to a single missing capability. Owner-inspectability is foreclosed because the privileged access an owner needs in order to inspect the system – to examine it from a clean vantage, to hunt a kernel-level rootkit or a vendor backdoor, and to let independent researchers work on hardware they own – is exactly the access that forfeits the device's attested standing. The capability that would dissolve this squeeze is what this paper calls a secure root: owner-controlled privileged inspection that surrenders neither verified boot nor the attestation a relying party accepts. This section asks whether such a capability exists. It proposes and evaluates no system; it systematizes the approaches that have been shipped or proposed, locates each against the verified-boot security model, and identifies the gap none of them closes – an open problem whose resolution would widen owner-inspectability well beyond the few who can tolerate the attestation penalty.

The most security-focused aftermarket systems reject root for precisely this reason. CalyxOS "does not support running in rooted mode, nor do we recommend this," on the ground that "Running any Android device with root permissions severely undermines the security of the device" [125]; the discontinued DivestOS likewise "does not support or encourage the use of root or runtime modification frameworks," which "break the trust model that AOSP employs and reduce the integrity of the system" [126]. That trust model is itself platform-centric: the Android platform security model requires agreement among user, platform, and developer rather than making the owner sovereign, and it classes rooting, "both intentional and malicious," as "a non-compliant change which violates CDD" – the Compatibility Definition Document a device must satisfy to ship as Android [127] – holding that ownership is "a legal concept rather than a technical one and therefore outside the scope of an OS security model" [15]. GrapheneOS, the furthest-developed case, has weighed the question directly, and the answer from its lead developer is more precise than a flat refusal: a carefully constrained root – "an on-device root terminal which requires a special boot mode and isn't persistent," limited to the user and barred from hijacking by apps – is "theoretically possible to do it in a way that doesn't throw away a lot of security," but "isn't being done by anyone right now"; the phrase "totally ruining verified boot by trusting persistent state" is directed instead at the persistent, fully-trusted way the root-enabled forks integrate it [128]. The project's own account put that cost plainly: once persistent state and the application layer are fully trusted, "the security model for verified boot and attestation are not intact to detect" a resulting compromise [129]. The boundedness of root established in Section 3 is thus not merely a restriction the stock vendor imposes and an aftermarket system could lift for free: a persistent root exacts a cost, and it falls on the owner, not the vendor. An owner can relock under a self-signed key and keep cryptographic verified boot even with root present [100], and the vendor-anchored attestation verdict that stock relying parties demand is in any case already forfeited by leaving the vendor's key behind, rooted or not; but a persistent, fully-trusted superuser defeats the verified-boot security model of not trusting persistent state, so the self-signed state the owner could otherwise check no longer tells them the device is untampered. That owner-side verifiability is what a persistent root costs, and a root that keeps it is, by these projects' own accounts, unbuilt where it is thought possible at all and rejected outright elsewhere. Hardware attestation is designed around exactly this: GrapheneOS's own documentation notes that the attestation API reports the device's state "in a way that even an attacker exploiting the OS after boot to gain root cannot trivially bypass" [75].

Restricting attention to what an owner can do while keeping the bootloader locked and verified boot engaged, the approaches differ on what actually varies among them (Table 4): whether they grant a full superuser, and whether they preserve the verified-boot security model under which the owner can still detect tampering. The pattern is that a full root forfeits that security model even on a locked, owner-signed device – a persistent, fully-trusted superuser is the compromise the model exists to catch – while the configurations that keep it are either non-persistent or not a full superuser at all.

Table 4. Owner root and privilege options that keep the bootloader locked and verified boot engaged.

Approach Full root? Verified-boot security model preserved (owner can detect tampering)?
Root baked into a signed image and relocked under an owner key: a Magisk-style systemless patch (avbroot [130], resign-android-image [100]) Yes No – a persistent, fully-trusted superuser
Scoped kernel root baked in the same way: KernelSU, with per-app profiles [131] Yes, scoped per app No – a persistent kernel-level superuser; app-profile scoping narrows the surface but is not a security boundary
Non-persistent root: a special-boot-mode terminal not retained across reboot [128] Only transiently Yes – the root does not persist across reboot, which restores the verified boot chain and system
Signed, verified extension shipped inside the image: Android APEX [132] (the Linux analogue, under a verity-and-signature image policy, is systemd-sysext [133]) No – bounded, policy-confined verified capability Yes – a signed, verity-checked image, so its contents are verified rather than arbitrary mutable state
Privileged but not root: ADB-shell brokering (Shizuku) [134] No – capped at the shell permission set Yes – stock image unmodified

Two qualifications attach to Table 4. The non-persistent row can be realized by a RAM-backed overlay, but an overlay's upper layer lies outside the verified-boot hashtree [76], so the content it serves is unverified whatever backs it; ephemerality bounds the window of unverified operation rather than keeping the running system verified. And the design space is not closed in principle: image-based operating systems have prompted proposals for an owner-facing "developer mode" that would reconcile locally built or signed code with an immutable, cryptographically validated system, but such a mode remains a design proposal rather than a shipping feature [135].

A concrete form makes the persistent-root row vivid. An owner could bake a root-accessible SSH daemon into the owner-signed image and authorize it with the very key that signs that image – the owner's verified-boot public key placed in the daemon's list of authorized keys, so that a single owner key governs both boot verification and administrative login while its private half stays off the device. Cryptographic verified boot is preserved and the credential story is clean, yet a persistent root service is exactly the fully-trusted persistent state the model is built to distrust – a verdict that holds whether it is reached locally or over the network, since what the model declines to trust is the persistent, fully-privileged state itself, not the transport that reaches it. A key-only daemon is in itself a mature and widely accepted surface; what the network transport adds is narrower – compromise no longer requires physical possession of the device, which leaves behind the on-device, physically-present case on which the safe reading depends. Gated instead to a non-persistent maintenance mode, it collapses into the non-persistent row.

Role separation sharpens the same conclusion. Confining administrative capability to a separate account or a deliberately entered maintenance session, while the owner's daily session runs unprivileged with no reachable escalation path, applies the principle of least privilege [136] and separation of duty [137] and keeps the everyday attack surface off the privileged path. But the account boundary alone does not preserve the verified-boot model: a persistent, writable administrative role is offline persistent root, so the model survives only if that maintenance context is itself ephemeral or re-sealed – its integrity re-measured against the owner's own key – on exit. In the owner-signed configuration the owner does hold that key and can re-seal [130]; the catch is operational: secure practice keeps the private half off the device (only the public key is enrolled), so re-sealing is an off-device re-sign and reflash from a trusted workstation rather than an in-situ maintenance step, and keeping the key on the device to make it in-situ would reintroduce the persistent trusted secret the locked chain exists to avoid. Such a re-seal restores the owner's own verified state, not the vendor-anchored attestation verdict, and no shipping system integrates it.

No approach in this design space, then, delivers all three of persistent owner administrative control, the verified-boot security model, and a relying-party-accepted attestation at once. The configurations that keep the security model do so by giving up persistence – the non-persistent root – or full privilege – a verified extension, or shell-tier brokering – while the one that keeps full persistent privilege under the owner's own key gives up the model and, with its non-vendor key, relying-party attestation. A capability that closed the gap would have to assemble three things the shipped approaches reach only in pairs: privileged inspection the owner can invoke; an integrity state the owner, and ideally an independent verifier, can still check afterward, which points to non-persistent or verified-extension privilege with an owner-held re-seal, subject to the off-device-key constraint above; and, for the relying-party half, an independent trust anchor for owner-enrolled keys that the attestation ecosystem does not presently provide. Each is individually plausible; none is assembled into a shipping system today. Treating that assembly as an open problem, rather than a settled impossibility, is what would let owner-inspectability – and with it independent malware and backdoor investigation – reach beyond the owners who can accept the attestation penalty.

14. Discussion

The limitations examined here are not independent defects but facets of a single design choice: administrative capability is withheld from the device owner and conferred only on the vendor and manufacturer. Verified boot, sandboxing, mandatory access control, attestation, and hardware-bound key storage each advance the platform's assurance that only approved, unmodified software runs, and each simultaneously removes a means by which an owner might inspect the device from a trusted vantage point. The circular trust dependency of Section 8 is the sharpest expression of the tension: the configurations an owner would need in order to verify the device are exactly those the platform refuses to attest as trusted.

The owner is consequently placed in a position analogous to that of an attacker with respect to introspection – indeed a worse one: these controls foreclose the owner's sole avenue – modifying the device to inspect it – while leaving open the runtime and sub-operating-system routes the capable adversary of Sections 8 and 12 uses, and the owner brings none of an attacker's willingness to damage the device. The practical recourses – JTAG-based memory acquisition, chip-level storage extraction, and exploit-driven temporary root – are, respectively, rarely available, destructive or specialized, and dependent on the existence of exploitable vulnerabilities that the platform is otherwise trying to eliminate. The physical-acquisition path is further foreclosed where unlocking the bootloader triggers a mandatory wipe of user data, so that gaining access to the storage also erases its contents [7]. None of these recourses offers the routine, non-destructive, owner-driven verification that the threat model of Section 3 calls for, and, as Sections 3 and 8 established, even a successful temporary root yields only a bounded in-system privilege on a device that has already forfeited its attested standing – not the external, trusted vantage point that verification requires. Nor would more privilege close the gap: a kernel-space rootkit manipulates the very kernel structures that any in-system observer, root included, must query, so it can neutralize a privileged security tool and falsify its results regardless of the privilege level at which that tool runs [47], [48]. Subversion-resistant detection must therefore observe the system from outside the running operating system [47], [138], echoing the long-established principle that a system cannot be trusted to report truthfully on its own state [117].

The contrast with a fully controlled host is one of category, not merely degree. On a desktop or server the baseline acquisition workflow – detach the storage and image it through a write blocker, a device that passes read commands while blocking any that would alter the drive, so the acquisition does not modify the evidence [5], [139], then decrypt the image with the owner's passphrase-derived key – is available to essentially any owner, and remains so even though the storage device itself runs opaque controller firmware that a determined attacker can subvert: compromising the firmware of a commercial off-the-shelf drive to backdoor data as it is written has been demonstrated using only public information and reverse engineering, installable by ordinary malware once the operating system is compromised [116], and such drive-firmware implants have been found in the wild [140], with persistence that survives disk formatting and a full operating-system reinstall [141]. Implants one layer lower still, in the motherboard's own UEFI flash, persist even across a storage replacement, because they do not reside on the storage at all [142]. That residual is real, but it is a different thing from the phone's barrier: an advanced and partially mitigable attack vector layered beneath an acquisition path that otherwise works, not a wall that forecloses the path for every owner. On a stock phone the same baseline workflow is foreclosed at its first step, because the storage is soldered, and at its last, because even a successful chip-level read returns the user's data as ciphertext under a hardware-bound key. The firmware-implant concern, common to both platforms and marking the floor of what either owner can verify, thus compounds on the phone a barrier that is already categorical rather than standing, as on the host, as the one residual beneath an otherwise working path.

Hardware memory acquisition sharpens the same contrast, but only partly, because it is closing on both sides. On a conventional computer an examiner can in principle capture RAM from outside the running operating system – by direct memory access over an expansion bus [143], [144] or by exploiting the residual charge in DRAM after a cold reboot [145] – yet modern platforms increasingly block such access with an input-output memory management unit [143], and cold-boot capture needs physical access to the memory. A stock phone forecloses even this residual avenue: its memory is soldered in package-on-package stacks that cannot be transplanted, it exposes no external bus capable of such access, and the one demonstrated on-device cold-boot variant first required unlocking the bootloader, which wipes the user data it sought to recover [146].

Table 5 sets the owner's control over each layer of the stack side by side for the two platforms, read downward from the bootloader to the firmware beneath the operating system. The pattern is a categorical difference across the upper, operating-system-and-boot layers, where the personal-computer owner holds administrative control and the stock-phone owner holds none, and a shared opaque floor at the firmware and management-coprocessor layers below them, where neither owner can inspect what runs.

Table 5. Owner control over the stack: traditional personal computer versus stock Android (as sold).

Stack layer Traditional personal computer (owner) Stock Android, as sold (owner)
Bootloader Replaceable; Secure Boot is optional, and the owner can enroll custom keys or disable it Locked and vendor-signed; unlocking wipes user data and drops attestation, and some devices are unlockable only by exploit or not at all
Kernel Owner builds and boots an arbitrary kernel Vendor-signed boot image; a custom kernel requires unlocking
Kernel modules Owner loads arbitrary modules Lockdown, module-signature, and dm-verity enforcement restrict loading
initramfs Owner controls Part of the signed boot image; not owner-modifiable on stock
init (first userspace, PID 1) Owner chooses or replaces the init system, and can boot to an alternate init or single-user mode Android init ships in the signed ramdisk and system partitions under verified boot and dm-verity, runs under SELinux, and is not owner-modifiable on stock
Operating system Owner installs any operating system A custom operating system requires unlocking and incurs an attestation penalty
In-system superuser (root) Available to the owner by default Withheld as sold; reachable only by exploit or unlocking, and then bounded by SELinux and kernel lockdown
Boot an external trusted system Yes, from external media Not supported while locked: the bootloader boots only signed images and an external system requires first unlocking [88], [7]; the path is then device-specific
Remove and image storage Yes: detach the storage and image it on a trusted controller Storage is soldered; chip-level reading is destructive, and the data returns as ciphertext under a hardware-bound key
Platform firmware BIOS/UEFI: reflashable but vendor-signed and opaque in practice, and in-the-wild implants have been demonstrated [142] Bootloader and vendor firmware: vendor-controlled and owner-opaque
Management co-processor Intel ME or AMD PSP: a vendor-firmware co-processor the owner cannot inspect – the ME embedded in the chipset with privileged access to platform data [147], the AMD-SP a boot-time root of trust that runs before the main cores [148] Cellular baseband, and any discrete secure element: vendor firmware on separate silicon the owner cannot inspect [111]
Storage-controller firmware Opaque; controller-firmware implants demonstrated in the lab [116] and found in the wild [140] Opaque

The division is systematic. On the personal computer the owner commands the entire operating-system-and-boot stack and is blocked only at the firmware and management-coprocessor floor; on the stock phone the owner commands essentially none of the stack, so the same firmware floor sits beneath a barrier that is already categorical at every layer above it. Administrative control, in the sense defined in Section 3, is exactly what the left column has and the right column lacks; root, where a phone owner reaches it, adds only the single "in-system superuser" row and leaves every other row unchanged.

The ease of this recourse is routinely overstated. The casual prescription to "just root it" presumes an act that retail devices are configured to resist: they ship with the bootloader locked, and unlocking it – where the vendor permits it at all – is gated behind an explicit warning and a mandatory wipe of user data [7], [64]. A large and well-documented class of carrier- and vendor-locked devices cannot be unlocked by their owners at all, or only by means of an exploit [89]. Unlocking is widely said to void the device warranty, although consumer-protection law in the United States and the European Union limits blanket voiding and requires a defect to be causally linked to the modification before coverage may be refused [149], [150]. Several mainstream vendors attach irreversible hardware-level consequences to unlocking, by distinct mechanisms rather than a single universal one: one permanently trips a one-time-programmable e-fuse that disables hardware-backed attestation and the protected features that depend on it and cannot be reset [151]; another irrevocably erases device-unique keys that relocking does not restore [152]; and one-time-programmable (eFuse) hardware is, more generally, the standard system-on-chip primitive for secure-boot enablement and anti-rollback enforcement, whose blowing is a one-way operation [153].

The honest counter-example is that not every platform is irreversible: on some devices unlocking can be reversed and the verified-boot and attestation state is restored on relocking – to the full state under the vendor's stock key, or to a reduced state under an owner-enrolled key [11], [60]. Even there the squeeze holds, because the reversible path returns the owner to the vendor-keyed configuration without ever granting the top attestation standing while the device remains open to inspection.

Taken together, these frictions make unlocking a high-barrier step rather than a routine one. The privileged state an owner does reach is, as Section 8 established, self-defeating for verification; and the cloaking tools owners deploy to pass integrity checks work only by impersonating a still-vulnerable stock device, leaving them locked in a steadily losing arms race against detection [110].

The unlock procedure is, moreover, not silent to software already resident on the device. Preparing a device for inspection changes observable system state, and unlocking the bootloader triggers a mandatory wipe that destroys the user-data partition before any image of it can be taken – so the inspection a high-threat owner attempts can itself alert, and then erase, a resident implant. That such environmental signals drive evasion is established rather than speculative: measurement studies show modern malware checks for virtualized or instrumented environments and withholds its behavior when it detects them [8], [9], and the anti-forensics literature names the matching capabilities of artifact wiping, trail obfuscation, and self-removal [10], [154]. Mobile spyware has combined the two in the wild: NSO's Pegasus for Android shipped "suicide functionality to remove itself" [155] (Suicide Functionality section), triggered among other cases when it cannot find a valid cellular subscriber identity – behavior attributed to avoiding analysis and emulator environments – while the iOS variant self-destructs when "a great probability of exposing the agent exists" [156] (Section 3.5), and later versions were observed deleting their own process records to hide their traces [45]. The specific loop – an implant watching for unlock preparation and erasing itself before acquisition – remains a reasoned extrapolation rather than a documented exploit; its constituent capabilities are each demonstrated, and the principle that a compromised system cannot be trusted to report truthfully on itself is long established [117], [138]. The nearest realized case, the Rombertik malware, destroys its host on detecting that its own code has been analyzed [157]; this is a genuine detect-then-destroy reaction, but it is keyed to tampering with the malware's own image rather than to a forensic acquisition, and it wrecks the host rather than quietly erasing the implant so the device passes inspection clean. No reported case closes the precise loop posited here.

Limitations of this analysis

Several limitations bound the claims made here. The paper is a systematization of existing evidence, not a new empirical study: it reports no measurements of its own, and where the literature is thin – notably on the precise prevalence of attestation-gated applications and on the fraction of devices for which hardware acquisition is feasible – it says so rather than substituting an estimate. Its central construct, owner-inspectability, is a qualitative criterion rather than a metric; this paper defines and applies it but does not quantify it, and an operational scale by which devices and configurations could be scored is left to future work. The analysis is deliberately scoped to the owner's standpoint and to the Android platform as shipped on mainstream devices; it does not weigh the owner-side costs against the genuine ecosystem-wide benefits that the same mechanisms deliver against running adversaries, which the platform literature documents [15], and it does not extend its specific claims to other platforms except where a cited source does so. Finally, the platform is a moving target: verdict tiers, acquisition techniques, and project capabilities change between releases, and the specific mechanisms cited here are current as of writing rather than permanent.

Inspectability and modifiability are distinct as ends – the criterion asks that the owner establish and demonstrate what the device runs, not that the device be freely modifiable – yet on locked stock devices they remain entangled in practice, in three ways. Mechanically, gaining a first inspection foothold on such a device generally requires the same unlock that also admits an arbitrary replacement system, so the capability the owner needs tends to arrive bundled with one the platform withholds. Through the software-freedom ecosystem, the freedoms to study, rebuild, and redistribute sustain inspection from upstream: auditable source and reproducible builds give the owner a known-good reference to check an acquired image against – they fix what a trusted build should contain, though confirming the device actually runs it still takes an acquired image or a trusted measurement – and shared tools and findings are what make inspection practical at all. And since inspectability is only a proxy for the owner's actual end – security for the owner, not the platform – modification can reach that end by another route: replacing an opaque firmware component with a more trustworthy build can improve security where inspecting it is impossible, though it substitutes a better-placed trust rather than delivering the verification the criterion measures, the same move as re-locking to a more transparent vendor's key (Section 12). That reaching inspection on a locked stock device usually routes through the broader modification the platform withholds is itself the case for decoupling the two by design.

A measured reading is that the platform optimizes for resistance to the ordinary running adversary at the cost of owner-side auditability, and that the two objectives, while not strictly incompatible, are in current designs rarely satisfied together. The forensic literature surveyed here does not claim that compromise is undetectable on stock devices; it claims that detection is constrained by observability, and that a negative result is accordingly weak evidence of integrity. Building on that, and on the user-controlled root of trust that AOSP allows in principle (Section 3) and the owner-signed GrapheneOS configuration of Section 12, this paper's own position is that auditability could be improved without abandoning existing protections. That position suggests a design space – owner-attestable inspection modes, exportable integrity measurements, or supported trusted-boot verification paths – in which verifiability and platform integrity might be advanced together rather than traded off.

15. Conclusion

Vendor-locked devices systematically limit the owner's ability to inspect, control, and independently verify the software they run. Stock Android, the most openly specified such platform and this paper's worked example, is the case developed here: the owner cannot practically examine the whole system from a clean, trusted environment; application and update delivery is mediated by centralized providers whose abuse could enable targeted malicious installation; internal storage and live memory are inaccessible without withheld privileges; attestation couples a device's attested standing to the device remaining unmodified; low-level rootkit detection generally demands a trusted memory snapshot taken from outside the running system; and the established techniques of host-based malware analysis are, as a class, unavailable without first breaking the verified-boot and attestation guarantees the platform enforces. Obtaining root does not lift these limits, because root on a hardened device is a bounded in-system privilege – not the full administrative control over the boot chain, kernel, and firmware that an owner would need – and reaching it forfeits the attested status the owner is trying to preserve. Backing up the hardware-bound encryption key is likewise impractical for most owners. The existence of consensual forensic tooling, and of hardened aftermarket operating systems such as GrapheneOS, does not overturn these conclusions: such tooling is bounded by the limited diagnostic data the platform exposes, owner-inspectable configurations are reachable only by leaving the as-sold device behind and paying an attestation penalty – the loss of device-integrity standing that leads a growing set of applications to refuse to run – to do so, and an absence of findings is accordingly weak evidence of integrity. These limits are not accidents of one vendor's engineering but consequences of vendor-lock itself, and the owner's structural position recurs, to varying degrees, on other vendor-locked devices. Treating security as owner-side verifiability, rather than as platform-side policy enforcement, makes these limitations visible as a coherent whole and identifies owner-inspectability as the property most in need of improvement.

Appendix A. GrapheneOS Auditor verified-boot key allowlist

Section 12's claim that the released GrapheneOS Auditor recognizes only keys compiled into it rests on the app's own source. Accepted verified-boot keys are fixed ImmutableMap<String, DeviceInfo> tables keyed by the hex SHA-256 of the verified-boot key: fingerprintsNonStock for the self-signed state and fingerprintsStock for the stock state, each with a StrongBox variant. The GrapheneOS release keys are hardcoded in the self-signed table [101]:

private static final ImmutableMap<String, DeviceInfo> fingerprintsNonStock = ImmutableMap
        .<String, DeviceInfo>builder()
        // GrapheneOS
        .put("F0A890375D1405E62EBFD87E8D3F475F948EF031BBF9DDD516D5F600A23677E8",
                new DeviceInfo(R.string.device_pixel_6, 100, 100, false, R.string.os_graphene))
        ...

Verification looks the attested key up in the table for the reported boot state and rejects any key that is absent, so a build signed with a key not compiled in – including an owner's self-signed build of otherwise unmodified GrapheneOS – is refused rather than attested:

final RootOfTrust.VerifiedBootState verifiedBootState = rootOfTrust.verifiedBootState;
final String verifiedBootKey = BaseEncoding.base16().encode(rootOfTrust.verifiedBootKey);
final DeviceInfo device;
if (verifiedBootState == RootOfTrust.VerifiedBootState.SELF_SIGNED) {
    if (attestationSecurityLevelEnum == ParsedAttestationRecord.SecurityLevel.STRONG_BOX) {
        device = fingerprintsStrongBoxNonStock.get(verifiedBootKey);
    } else {
        device = fingerprintsNonStock.get(verifiedBootKey);
    }
} else if (verifiedBootState == RootOfTrust.VerifiedBootState.VERIFIED) {
    if (attestationSecurityLevelEnum == ParsedAttestationRecord.SecurityLevel.STRONG_BOX) {
        device = fingerprintsStrongBoxStock.get(verifiedBootKey);
    } else {
        device = fingerprintsStock.get(verifiedBootKey);
    }
} else {
    throw new GeneralSecurityException("verified boot state is not verified or self signed");
}

if (device == null) {
    throw new GeneralSecurityException("invalid verified boot key fingerprint: " + verifiedBootKey);
}

At the time of writing, GrapheneOS publishes no user-facing procedure for adding or replacing an accepted verified-boot key with an owner's own – its device-support tutorial covers only submitting a locked-stock sample for GrapheneOS itself to add a new factory device, not an owner or alternative-OS key [97], [158]. It states only that an alternative operating system's verified-boot key must be "included in the Auditor app and Attestation Server." Recognizing an owner-signed build therefore means editing these hardcoded tables in the source and rebuilding the Auditor app: local second-device verification needs only that [158], while scheduled remote verification [158] additionally requires rebuilding the app to point at a different server – the released Auditor pins attestation.app and rejects any other [159], [160] – and self-hosting a correspondingly keyed attestation server [98].

Two observations from practice bear this out. An owner who locks the bootloader to their own AVB key and tries to enable remote verification against the official service is turned away with an HTTP 400 [161]. And where an owner-rooted key is accepted at all, it is by forking both components: DiamaneOS, a downstream build, ships its own key allowlists, externalizes the trusted keys to a replaceable configuration, and adds a second trust profile that accepts a device reporting self-signed verified boot whose key chains to no manufacturer root – generalized owner-key attestation, but gated by that project's own release list and the account holder's approval rather than offered as an end-user facility [162]; the robotnix build system similarly patches the Auditor app and attestation server to use owner-created keys, automating the owner-signed OS together with a matching app and server [163].
